Leah Stewart, 34, a teacher and mother of a one-year-old, was attacked by the shark while on a morning swim at Coogee beach in Sydney’s eastern suburbs on 13 June. She remained in a critical condition for more than two weeks while receiving treatment for life-threatening injuries that required the amputation of her arm. I’ll never forget its face,” she said. “It sort of started opening its mouth and I’m like, ‘it’s going to get my face … I’ve got to try and punch it. I’ve got to try and push it away or else it’s going to bite my head off’.” Being right-handed, Stewart said the split-second decision to deliver “a left hook” came after asking herself: “Which limb am I willing to lose?” Stewart said the following moments happened “in slow motion”, describing it as “like fighting a dinosaur”. “In my head I was like, ‘you ugly fucker, you are not taking me away from my daughter’, and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again,” she said. “It was so big. cards.summary: 路易斯安那州即将开启50多年来首次休闲鳄鱼狩猎季，最多允许5000名猎人在严格规则下捕捉鳄鱼。该州曾在1962年因过度捕猎导致鳄鱼数量降至不足10万只而全面禁猎，如今其数量已恢复至约300万只。

cards.source_text: The first recreational alligator hunt in Louisiana in more than half a century is about to commence in the swamps of that state, with up to 5,000 hopeful trappers facing strict rules in order to snare a reptile. The state’s fish and wildlife commission banned alligator hunting in 1962 to allow the species to recover after decades of unregulated killings for meat and hides dropped numbers there to below 100,000. Now, with the population above an estimated 3 million in the wild, Louisiana is issuing public permits to licensed hunters for a month-long season beginning 1 October, across eight zones statewide. Although alligator hunting has taken place since an outright 10-year ban ended in 1972, it had been restricted to tightly regulated commercial harvesting, making this the first time the public has been able to legally snare for fun or sport a creature embedded in Louisiana’s culture and history. “Louisiana now has a robust alligator resource capable of providing sustainable recreational harvest opportunities to Louisiana residents without negatively impacting a highly valuable commercial industry that provides more than $250m annually to Louisiana’s economy,” the Louisiana department of wildlife and fisheries (LWF) said in a statement accompanying details of the hunt. Applicants have until Monday to enter a lottery for up to two per person of 5,000 tags that will allow them to hunt an alligator, with state residents paying $25 and visitors $150 for each zone they visit, on top of a $50 application fee. The hunt has been designated strictly non-commercial, meaning that those who trap one cannot sell the meat or skin. Applicants must already possess a basic hunting license issued by LWF, and are restricted to hook and line trapping, meaning they cannot use poles or other methods favored by poachers. Firearms can only be used to kill captured alligators, not for shooting free-swimming reptiles. The hunt brings Louisiana broadly into line with Florida, another state that said its conservation programs allowed alligator numbers to recover to the point where recreational hunting is permitted. Florida introduced a similarly regulated statewide program in 1988.
cards.source_title: Louisiana gears up for first recreational alligator hunt in more than 50 years

In 2015, the remote coastal fjords of southern Patagonia turned into a whale graveyard. That June, scientists found 337 dead and decomposing sei whales, a species of baleen whale, on the beaches between the Gulf of Penas and Puerto Natales in Chile. Researchers flew over the area, then took samples from the rotting bodies, trying to find clues as to why this happened. It was later reported to be the largest mass baleen whale mortality event on record. Data collected to determine the cause proved inconclusive, however. Scientists thought the most likely explanation was a toxic red tide provoked by pollution, a strong El Niño event and climate change. More than 10 years later, Clarke and her BAS colleagues not only use satellite imagery to identify different whale species by observing flippers and flukes in the water, but can spot whale strandings almost anywhere in the world. cards.source_text: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among mangroves. Over 18 months, they sampled 20 sites, collecting the calls of gibbons, frogs, hornbills, insects, and other wildlife. They want to establish a baseline before Nusantara, Indonesia’s new capital city, alters the surrounding landscape, according to a video produced by Mongabay, Scientific American, and Project Multatuli. Nusantara is being built in East Kalimantan province to relieve some of Jakarta’s congestion and pressure from land subsidence. Its planners describe a “smart forest city” where development and biodiversity can coexist. Roads, apartment buildings, a hotel, and a presidential palace have already appeared. Construction and chainsaws are becoming part of the local soundscape. The recordings will allow scientists to compare conditions over time. They may show where species remain, where they decline, and whether development is pushing wildlife into other areas. The findings could also help identify places where conservation measures are most needed. The project also records knowledge held by the Indigenous Balik people. Animal calls have long helped them interpret the forest. Gibbons marked the approach of dawn and, in unusual circumstances, were thought to warn of a death in the village. The great argus (Argusianus argus), a large pheasant native to the island’s forests, held particular importance. Some younger Balik children no longer recognize its call. Local residents have helped select recording sites, explain the history of the landscape, and describe the connections between certain species, places, and customs. Abidin, who was born in Pemaluan and has never left, said he hopes the recordings will help him teach his children about the forest. He said he worries they may have to adjust to urban life without the education or skills needed to find work there. The researchers said they do not expect the project to stop Nusantara’s construction. Nor can the recordings preserve the forest or document every part of Balik culture. cards.source_text: - The Great African Seaforest is one of the only expanding kelp forests in the world. To better understand this important ecosystem, and why it should be conserved, marine biologist Loyiso Dunga set out to map the entire forest for the first time ever in 2016 using satellite imagery. - Dunga now works on kelp forest conservation across the globe with both the International Union for Conservation of Nature and the Kelp Forest Alliance. - As a member of an Indigenous community in South Africa, Dunga is sensitive to how conservation measures were employed during the country’s apartheid-era to expel coastal communities, and makes sure that other scientists include coastal communities in their work. - “There is so much knowledge that is documented within coastal communities but is outside of science,” Dunga says. “I try to spend a lot of time understanding that, which also enriches my science.” CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As a member of the Xhosa nation, the ocean was kin or family to Dunga, and a sacred place. But that snorkeling trip was the first time he went into the ocean for fun. “That moment enchanted me,” said Dunga, who lives in Cape Town. Dunga’s research is now focused on evaluating kelp ecosystems. He works in South Africa as the executive director for the Seas of Good Hope program and globally with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the Kelp Forest Alliance, a group that is dedicated to protecting over 9 million acres (3.6 million hectares) of kelp forests by 2040. But, for this conservation work to succeed, Dunga says that Indigenous wisdom, science and policy must be better connected. Dunga founded Asili Blue Renaissance, a nonprofit, to provide diverse, legitimate ocean conservation measures, including working with Indigenous communities. Dunga is now working on an initiative with the Kelp Forest Alliance to rename global kelp forests by their Indigenous names. Mongabay spoke with Dunga on the phone about his work. cards.source_text: It’s hard to imagine that the space-crazed general public needed any help getting worked up about astronauts and NASA in the early ’60s. Perhaps the wild popularity of space-related imagery was in part what motivated NASA administrator James Webb to create the NASA Art Program in 1962. Although the program’s handpicked artists weren’t edited or censored in any way, they were briefed on how NASA hoped to be represented, and which emotions their creations were meant to capture—the excitement and uncertainty of exploring these frontiers. NASA was also careful to collect everything the artists produced while participating in the program, from sketches to finished work. In turn, the artists received unprecedented access to launch sites, key personnel, and major events such as Project Mercury and the Apollo 11 Mission. Hundreds of artists, including Andy Warhol, Norman Rockwell, and Laurie Anderson, have brought their unique sensibilities to the project. (Find NASA-inspired art by Warhol and Rockwell above.) (And hey, no shame if you mistakenly assumed Warhol’s 1987 Moonwalk 1 was created as a promo for MTV…) Jamie Wyeth’s 1964 watercolor Gemini Launch Pad includes a humble bicycle, the means by which technicians traveled back and forth between the launch pad and the reinforced-concrete blockhouse where they worked. Photographer Annie Leibovitz offers two views of NASA’s first female pilot and commander, Eileen Collins—with and without helmet. Postage stamp designer, Paul Calle, one of the inaugural group of participating artists, produced a stamp commemorating the Gemini 4 space capsule in celebration of NASA’s 9th anniversary. When the Apollo 11 astronauts suited up prior to blastoff on July 16, 1969, Calle was the only artist present. His quickly rendered felt-tip marker sketches lend a backstage element to the heroic iconography surrounding astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins. One of the items they carried with them on their journey was the engraved printing plate of Calle’s 1967 commemorative stamp. They hand-canceled a proof aboard the flight, on the assumption that post offices might be hard to come by on the moon. In 2016, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory enlisted a team of nine artists, designers, and illustrators to collaborate on 14 posters, a visual throwback to the ones the WPA created between 1938 and 1941 to spark public interest in the National Parks. cards.source_text: It doesn’t quite ring true to call David Bowie a rock star. Ziggy Stardust, the neon synthetic-clad alien alter ego he both created and retired in the early seventies, was, of course, rock stardom outlandishly personified. But then, that was the concept of what turned out to be just one of many personae he deliberately crafted throughout the course of his career. That career was in music, primarily, but looking back on it today, more than a decade after Bowie’s death, it looks more like his medium was culture itself. That’s underscored by his interviews, clips from a variety of which appear in the new video above from YouTube channel T&H Inspiration. Most of T&H’s most popular videos add visuals to speeches by the popularizer of Eastern philosophy Alan Watts, who’s been featured here on Open Culture before. He and Bowie had more in common than it may seem at first, beginning with an Englishness that remained thoroughgoing no matter how far out they ventured into the world. Though Watts’ interest in Buddhism hardly needs stating, it’s worth remembering that he chose to be ordained as an Episcopalian priest rather than as a Buddhist monk. The young Bowie, for his part, very nearly took the latter path, studying under the late Lama Chime Rinpoche, who eventually told him he’d be better off going into the music business. Bowie did so, of course, but with a new “sense of transience and change, which actually became fundamental to my life and my approach to it,” as he put it decades later. That sense manifests even in his early work, but embracing and even pursuing impermanence — the impermanence of sounds, of fashions, of hit records, of life itself — also kept him from getting mired in the irrelevance or auto-kitsch that threatens every superstar. Given the belief that nothing lasts forever, “looking for the source of one’s own being becomes much more important,” as does attempting artistic or intellectual challenges at the very edge of one’s abilities. Alan Watts would probably have agreed. The bigger question is, did he ever hear “Changes”? cards.source_text: The sign asks us not to disturb the birds. Understandable. It’s easy to miss the nests a couple of feet above your head until your hair’s parted by an incoming house martin. They slalom the red sandstone ruins, metallic blue flashes in the morning sun. Occasionally one jinks up to the corner, disappears into the nest to meet the needs of demanding mouths, emerges and darts away again, a sleek silhouette against a backdrop of water. Tantallon Castle has perched on a promontory overlooking the Firth of Forth for 700 years. For more than half that time it’s been a ruin, besieged by Oliver Cromwell and never repaired. Its remnants are home to dozens of house martins. Their national numbers are in shocking decline, but here they retain a stronghold. They build their mud cups – marvels of engineering held together with saliva and hope – raise their broods, then wing it back to Africa, their exact wintering location still largely mysterious. Their ancestors saw battles and banquets. Now their summers play out to a gentle flow of tourists. A mile across the water sits Bass Rock – a quietly monumental, broad-shouldered icon, its distinctive shape speckled white with birds and guano. To Bass Rock, the castle’s a mere whippersnapper. With 340m years under its belt, it’s seen everything. Mainly it’s seen gannets, whose scientific name, Morus bassanus, bears evidence of the close association. Around 100,000 call it home – it used to be more, but bird flu has denuded their population since it hit in 2022. A recent study by the RSPB (now the island’s owners) and Aarhus University reckons it will take the population at least 15 years to recover. For the survivors, a strange remnant: their vivid blue irises turn black. Across the water they swarm the island like midges, wheeling round in broad arcs. Up, turn, pause, tuck wings, plunge – sleek bullets producing the merest splash. Around me the martins snap up invisible insects in midair. These hunting skills are virtually mystical to us, second nature to them. Survival is hard, and getting harder. But give these birds half a chance and they’ll rebound. Half a chance – it’s better than none at all.

When the sludge metal giants fired their troubled but brilliant guitarist in March 2025, it was the culmination of a long, doomed effort to pull him back from the edge—to get him sober, to reengage him with his love of music, to help him move past his petty, self-sabotaging resentments. Even after the split, his bandmates hoped it would just be a temporary break. “We were certain that two months later, two years later, we were going to have the high five—I’m sorry, dude. I’m sorry, too, man. I love you,” bassist Troy Sanders told GQ earlier this year. That never happened. Hinds died in a motorcycle crash in Atlanta on August 20, 2025. Two weeks later, Mastodon started recording their ninth album, Marrow Deep. Even more than most metal bands, Mastodon have long wrestled with personal tragedy and grief in their music. 2009’s uncompromisingly progressive Crack the Skye was inspired in part by the suicide of drummer Brann Dailor’s sister, Skye, and its more streamlined follow-up, The Hunter, found Hinds reckoning with the death of his brother. Emperor of Sand spun an extended metaphor about cancer, which had just killed guitarist Bill Kelliher’s mom. Marrow Deep was intended to deal with Dailor’s mother’s suffering from rheumatoid arthritis and her death at the end of 2024. By the time they entered the studio, it inevitably became about Hinds, too. The wild, untamed spark he once brought to Mastodon will be much missed, but his absence also means Marrow Deep finds the band as functional as they’ve been in years. After the disappointment of 2021’s bloated Hushed and Grim, an album that Hinds barely contributed to, they sound like they’re back on the right track. No score yet, be the first to add. They kept their songwriting uncomplicated and stripped back their live shows to a four-piece kit. But they used their simplicity to their advantage; knowing only half of what they wanted to sound like, they could toy with the rest until they found their magic. With their debut EP, 2025’s This Better Be Something Great, Westside Cowboy claimed the mantle of what they called “Britainicana,” adapting country inspirations to a “stock”—their word—indie-rock sound. The rootsy influence was clearest in the closers on their EPs, taking the form of languorous melodic ballads featuring either a prominent cowpoke drawl (“Slowly, I’m Sure”) or cooing doo-wop harmony (“In the Morning”). But they quickly sidestepped their self-imposed label. No score yet, be the first to add. Their debut LP, It Goes On, doubles as Westside Cowboy’s coming-of-age story. Musically, it captures their quickly gained confidence; they bob in and out of their influences easily, taking advantage of whatever propels them. Opener “Kick Stones (The Boys)” evokes the Velvet Underground’s “What Goes On,” molding its fuzzy guitar into a faster, sharper melody that crescendos restlessly. Likewise, zippy Vampire Weekend guitar trills infuse the bouncy instrumental breakdown of “Paperchains,” which jolts the band out of its melancholic depiction of graying from boredom. cards.source_text: Admit it, you miss me. María Isabel Severino is certain of that on her new post-relationship glow-up EP, Miss Me Much? As an aspiring star at a performing arts high school, she taped Alicia Keys posters in her locker and studied the sepia-toned R&B you might’ve once owned on CD. In 2021, she released two tender and subdued EPs, Stuck in the Sky and i hope you’re very unhappy without me. Now, she’s linked up with El Guincho, known for his career-making work with Rosalía, to produce her third. On a 20-minute tessellation of Latin pop flecked with dembow, reggaeton, Jersey club, and hip-hop, María Isabel aims to graduate from ingénue to icon. It’s an unexpected appearance from the Spanish producer, a key player in the globalization of reggaeton who’s logged firestarting collaborations with alt-pop divas like Bjӧrk, Charli xcx, FKA twigs, and Amaarae, as well as executive-producing Camila Cabello’s hotly debated C,XOXO. With a flair for coaxing singers out of their comfort zones, his work teeters between brilliance and blasphemy, overproduced yet outré, in spite of its popular appeal. As a rising artist, María Isabel represents a fresh Caribeña canvas, with a delicate vocal tone that requires a light touch. No score yet, be the first to add. Rather than go to extremes, on Miss Me Much? María Isabel embraces classic textures and references, penning brisk melodies from the piano bench and situating island attitude against concrete romanticism. A minimal bassline fades into the noir gloaming of Auto-Tuned opener “Sunset Tower,” which invokes the historic Hollywood building. Capturing a relationship near its end, the song shares DNA with “Nikes” and a touch of “No More Parties in LA”: Not even dinner at Carbone or a glass of Moët can mask these feelings. Even more dramatic is “1-800,” as vaporous as heat off pavement. Co-written with Amaarae collaborator Mason “Maesu” Tanner, it’s the EP’s only English-language song, a spotlight for her pristine vocal technique. The hook, “834-8965/I wanna catch on one of these vibes,” accentuated by synthetic chimes and bumping, blunted drums, makes me want to crawl on the floor. Even in its simplicity, this song has contours. When the tempo picks up, the production doesn’t veer too far afield. The popularity of Jersey club can make it feel like an experimental shortcut (especially by artists who aren’t from the East Coast) but “Bien Bien” pulls it off like designer. cards.source_text: A dinky piano motif opened “Playing Yoself,” a brief tune that came out last year. It was the slightest song on Liim Lasalle Loves You, the debut album from the titular 22 year old, who then made an observation—“I be singing like I’m the nigga playing the piano”—that doubled as a declaration of intent. Liim is precocious and charming, an A+ pupil in the school of lovesick prodigies: pained brothers swooning—or seething—on pianos grand and small, from Stevie Wonder striking organs to Odd Future mashing MIDI controllers. But Liim is not always a pianist, not always a singer: He perceives music “differently,” and proves it by performing it in a variety of ways. He spent his adolescence in Harlem, gorging skate videos and “different-ass shit” like “Smashing Pumpkins and Kodak Black.” Now as an adult, his motley influences have congealed toward latter-day L.A.: the smirking lust of Steve Lacy, the zany chops of the Internet, and the lovelorn streak of Tyler, the Creator, who—have you heard?—is a really big fan. As a Brooklynite with a Pacific bent, Liim is bicoastally appealing, although his skill transcends those binaries. He sings over lush chords and hydraulic basslines, in a breezy lilt that deepens when he raps, in effortlessly jiggy spurts. It is a testament to his musicality that it often covers for his limited message, with “Playing Yoself” being a paradigmatic example: “Wondering what’s up with me... cards.source_text: Take a look at photos of Bush Tetras — a three-girl-one-guy No Wave/Post-Punk band from the early 1980s downtown Manhattan scene. Now, look at the photograph above, “Marcel Breuer and His Harem,” by Bauhaus photographer Erich Consemüller, taken sometime around 1927. Except for the fact that Breuer looks more like Ron Mael of Sparks sans mustache than drummer Dee Pop, one might mistake this for a photo of the punk band. This raises a few questions: did art students Bush Tetras look to the women of the Bauhaus for their style? Or did the women of the Bauhaus look to the future and see punk? The second scenario seems more likely since the women of the Bauhaus have not, until recently, been terribly well-known. I personally feel cheated after studying art and art history in college many years ago and only now getting introduced to several significant artists of the radical German art school founded by Walter Gropius. All of its famous exponents and art stars are men, but it seems the gender ratio of the Bauhaus was closer to that of the general population (as was, in many cases, that of the early punk and post-punk scenes). But we don’t tend to learn the names or see the work of these artists, and, in some cases, their work has been posthumously attributed to their male colleagues. Nor are we familiar with their progressive personal style, essential in the Bauhaus’s total approach to revolutionizing the arts, including fashion, as a way to liberate humanity from the dogmas of the past. How unfortunate that the memory of the Bauhaus, like the memory of punk, replicated the same old rules its artists broke. The school’s gender equality was radical, hence the photograph’s satirical title, which “expresses the precise opposite of what the photo itself shows,” notes the site Bauhaus Kooperation: “the modernity, emancipation, equality, or even superiority, of the women in it.” The “junior master” of the carpentry workshop, Breuer looks at the three artists to his left “skeptically, with his arms crossed,” as if to say, “ ‘These are ‘my’ women?!’ ” The artists of the “harem,” from left to right, are Breuer’s wife Martha Erps, Katt Both, and the photographer’s wife, Ruth Hollós, who “seems to be suppressing laughter as she looks towards the photographer (her husband).” Erich Consemüller, who taught architecture at the Bauhaus, had been tasked by Gropius with documenting the school and its life. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 28 minute listen In May 2010, I was invited to Brunei to give two lectures on agriculture. At the time, the government there had just launched a plan to become more self-sufficient in rice production to promote greater ‘food security’ – a goal Brunei still holds today, along with greater ‘sustainability’. After one of my lectures, I was asked by a journalist what I thought of the plan. My sense at the time was that this plan was wrongheaded, and I said so. Brunei is a tiny, super-wealthy sultanate composed mainly of tropical rainforest on the ecologically fragile island of Borneo. The country’s wealth was (and still is) based overwhelmingly on oil and natural gas. I suggested that the sultanate carry on with carbon, and purchase the rice it needed from neighbouring countries in Southeast Asia, which is, after all, the buckle of the world’s rice belt. In other words, pursue your comparative advantage, rather than divert resources to produce a cheap, basic commodity relatively inefficiently on bad soil in an unsuitable setting. Alas, the country is still plugging away on its rice plan, which hasn’t gone all that well. After years of assiduous efforts and considerable investment, in 2024 Brunei produced 8 per cent of the rice it consumed, up from 4.8 per cent in 2017, which means it is still a long way from self-sufficiency. Fortunately for Bruneians, the sultanate easily gets all the rice it needs from neighbouring countries, as Southeast Asia has long been a rice-surplus region. I would argue that, if Brunei remains insistent on achieving greater self-sufficiency in rice, it would do better to buy or lease farmland and hire agriculturalists elsewhere to grow rice for the sultanate than try to raise rice for itself. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 20 minute listen Here is something we have never quite said out loud: for a significant portion of the world’s women, hunger is not a temporary state. It is a cognitive condition. It flows beneath everything: the meeting, the conversation, the stream of thought that almost ran its course before something more insistent pulled it back. For many of us, the state of hunger was present since we were old enough to understand that our bodies were under review. I was 11. I was sitting beside a swimming pool that summer, the one before middle school started, trying to follow a conversation I kept losing. I had decided, with the particular certainty children sometimes develop about the rules of the world they are entering, that I would eat as little as possible before sixth grade. The plan involved a sleeve of SnackWell’s cookies per day: fat-free, engineered to taste like cardboard, manufactured specifically for women and girls who had been told that fat was the enemy and desire was something to be managed rather than answered. The SnackWell’s cookie was itself a cultural artefact, a product designed to help women comply with an instruction they had already internalised. It did not quiet the hunger, because hunger is not a preference. It is biology doing what biology does when a body is not fed, sending signals that push everything else aside. During the day, we swam, lay on the concrete, and talked about the coming year. My attention kept sliding away from the conversation. A thought would begin and dissolve into the same insistent loop: how long until dinner, how little I could manage when it arrived, whether anyone had noticed what my body was doing without my permission. I remember listening to a teammate tell a long story and realising I had not heard most of it. Something louder had taken the space the story needed. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything. When the novel begins, David and his assistant Cody are aboard a private jet flying from his home in the US to the UK. Landing at London City airport (which the book, experiencing its own senior moment, situates in the countryside), they visit David’s daughter and her family before travelling on to Zurich (hence “Switzy”). One more appointment, a catchup with an old boarding school roommate called Tom, awaits just over the French border, after which David will be euthanised at a facility resembling Dignitas. David is wealthy. Not wealthy enough to own the jet he’s flying around in – that’s a loan from his boss – but someone to whom its polished doors, “that slid silently and obligingly out of sight”, are of a piece with the comfortable, largely frictionless world through which he moves. He has had a career in business, chief financial officer of some undefined entity – one large enough for a forensic accounting firm to be required when it became apparent David, in an early sign of the seriousness of his impairment, had mistakenly scattered its money into “an archipelago of overseas accounts”. For all the capital he has accumulated, David has been “a support person, a man whose name would never be known”, who sat at a desk and “made certain numbers swell up and other numbers recede”. Having successfully led the global response to the financial crash of 2008, and advocated powerfully during the pandemic for global cooperation against the virus, he was never going to simply sit back and shrug as the world spiralled into conflict and chaos under Donald Trump. But still, I thought, as I opened his latest book on the collapse of the old world order, it’s barely three years since his last tome on fixing the general mess (Permacrisis, written with the economists Mohammed El-Erian and Michael Spence). cards.source_text: In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983). Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex. The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since. As each one came out I tore through them: not just because Jane was brilliant and I was a fan, but also because she was my aunt. My grandmother, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, had been Jane’s mother-in-law: mother of Peter Scott and of my father Wayland Young. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. It put my smoky-voiced, glamorous aunt and me in a peculiar overlap: she, in her 60s, was writing a fictional version of the actual life she had lived, and I, at 29, was writing a putatively factual version of the same things, though they had happened before I was born. That was my first book; the last Cazalet novel was to be Jane’s last. cards.summary: 哲学家阿莎·莉娜·班达里从爱荷华大学转至石溪大学，获得哲学系教授和医学院照护伦理研究教授及副主席的双重任命。她将于明日正式履新。班达里以关怀伦理和自主性研究闻名，其跨学科任命体现了哲学与医学的融合趋势。
cards.relevant: 班达里的跨院系任职反映了当代哲学研究向应用伦理转向，尤其在医疗照护领域，对学科发展具有示范意义。
cards.context: 班达里在爱荷华大学任教多年，其著作《自由去关怀》探讨自由主义框架下的依赖与关怀问题。石溪大学医学院设有医学人文学中心，需要哲学背景的学者推动伦理研究。
cards.source_analysis: Daily Nous是哲学界知名新闻网站，报道客观，主要面向专业哲学家群体。
cards.social_impact: 哲学与医学的交叉任命可能促进医疗伦理实践，尤其在老龄化社会背景下，关怀伦理的现实意义日益凸显。

items.title: Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
items.summary: The articles that made it into the latest edition of Philosophers Annual have been announced. The list aims to “select the ten best articles published in philosophy each year—an attempt as simple to state as it is admittedly impossible to fulfill.” This volume—the 45th—covers the literature from 2024. The selections are: Evan Behrle (Harvard), “Desert and Economic Interdependence” from the Journal of Philosophy. Outside of philosophy, the idea that workers deserve to be paid according to their productive contributions is very popular. But political philosophers have given it relatively little attention. In this paper, I argue against the attempt to use this idea about desert and contribution to vindicate significant income inequality. I claim that reward according to contribution fails on its own terms when the following condition holds: the size of each worker’s contribution depends on what other workers only together do. When workers only together make another more productive, that is not reflected in the sum of their own contributions. Thus reward according to contribution recognizes individual accomplishments without recognizing their dependence on collectives, dependence that is, in complex economies, ubiquitous. Sam Berstler (MIT), “The Structure of Open Secrets” from the Philosophical Review. In conversation, we often do not acknowledge what we jointly know to be true. This article identifies a distinctive kind of non-acknowledgment norm, open secrecy norms, and analyzes how such norms constrain our speech. Open secrecy norms iterate: when is an open secret, then there’s a norm not to acknowledge that ⁠, and this norm is itself an open secret. items.title: Switzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly moving
items.summary: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinic The word “Alzheimer’s” never appears in Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, which arrives pre-endorsed as a Booker prize longlistee. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything. When the novel begins, David and his assistant Cody are aboard a private jet flying from his home in the US to the UK. Landing at London City airport (which the book, experiencing its own senior moment, situates in the countryside), they visit David’s daughter and her family before travelling on to Zurich (hence “Switzy”). One more appointment, a catchup with an old boarding school roommate called Tom, awaits just over the French border, after which David will be euthanised at a facility resembling Dignitas. items.title: ‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet Chronicles
items.summary: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off? In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983). Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex.
